title: Unit Testing Typed Functions knowledge check

questions.prompt: What makes a function type useful?
options: It automatically tests the function at runtime.
It causes the function to run when the type is declared.
It replaces all runtime error handling.
It documents parameter and return contracts so callers and implementations can be checked consistently.
questions.answer_key: It documents parameter and return contracts so callers and implementations can be checked consistently.
questions.explanation: Function types are compile-time contracts and should be paired with behavior tests.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Unit Testing Typed Functions”?
options: A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
The concept should be demonstrated with testing inputs and outputs and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with testing inputs and outputs and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Testing inputs and outputs”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Unit Testing Typed Functions”?
options: Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check boundary conditions, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
Assume testing failure cases is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
questions.answer_key: Check boundary conditions, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Boundary conditions”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
